konglak-para.desc: Most visitors to Sajek stay around the main cottage strip, but Konglak sits at the very end of the ridge. A short, steep climb through bamboo brings you to a quiet village of stilted houses, with orange and other fruit trees around. The views from here stretch over the Mizoram hills, and sunrise is quieter than at the helipad.
blocks: How to get there
Walk or take a short jeep ride to the end of the Sajek road, then climb about 30–45 minutes.
Good to know
Respect villagers' privacy, ask before photos, and buy fruit or tea locally.

kathin-chibar-dan.desc: At the end of the rainy-season retreat, Buddhists offer new robes to monks. At Rajban Vihara the offering is made in a demanding traditional way: cotton is spun, woven, dyed and sewn into a robe within twenty-four hours, with women working through the night on looms. Huge crowds gather from across the hill tracts, making it one of the largest Buddhist gatherings in Bangladesh.
blocks: Good to know
Dates follow the lunar calendar; check locally. Expect big crowds and dress modestly.

glance: 310 km to Rangamati by road, 8–10 hours by bus or car
kaptai-national-park.desc: Kaptai National Park was declared in 1999 and covers about 5,465 hectares of mixed evergreen forest around Kaptai in Rangamati district. Teak and garjan plantations, some planted in colonial times, cover the hills above the Karnaphuli River just below the Kaptai dam. Short forest walks, watchtowers and riverside spots make it a quiet day out, and elephants, monkeys and many birds live in the wider forest. The road from Chattogram to Kaptai along the river is itself very pretty.
blocks: How to get there
From Rangamati take a bus or CNG to Kaptai (about 1.5 hours), or come directly from Chattogram by bus to Kaptai.
Good to know
Stay on marked trails and do not enter the forest at dusk; wild elephants live in the area.

glance: 310 km to Rangamati by road, 8–10 hours by bus or car
Hire a boat; about 1,500–3,000 BDT per day depending on size (approx.)
kaptai-lake.desc: Kaptai Lake was formed in the early 1960s when the Karnaphuli river was dammed for hydroelectric power. The rising water flooded valleys and villages, including much of old Rangamati, and displaced many Chakma families, a history worth remembering on the water. Today it is a vast, winding lake of hilltop islands, floating markets and fishing boats. A day on a hired boat takes in villages, island restaurants and waterfalls.
blocks: How to get there
Buses from Chattogram reach Rangamati in about 2.5–3 hours; boats are hired at Reserve Bazar or the Parjatan area.
Good to know
Wear life jackets. Foreigners need prior permission to enter the Chittagong Hill Tracts. Check the latest government advisories before travelling.

glance: BFDC fish landing ghat in Rangamati town for fresh catch; rice hotels in Rangamati town and lakeside island restaurants
kaptai-lake-kachki-chapila.desc: Kaptai Lake is one of the country's biggest freshwater fisheries, and its catch is dominated by small fish like kachki and chapila. Rangamati's hotels fry them crisp or cook them as a dry chorchori with onion and green chilli, eaten with rice; you will also find rui and other carp from the lake. Each year fishing is closed for about three months from late April to let the fish breed, so the freshest small fish are on menus from mid-August onward.

glance: 310 km to Rangamati by road, 8–10 hours by bus or car
rangamati-tribal-cultural-museum.desc: The Tribal Cultural Institute was set up in Rangamati in 1978 to preserve the cultures of the Chakma, Marma, Tripura and other peoples of the Chittagong Hill Tracts. Its museum shows traditional dresses, jewellery, weapons, coins, wooden and metal statues, musical instruments and handicrafts. Look for the old palm-leaf manuscripts and the map showing where each community lives. It is a good first stop before exploring the lake and villages.
blocks: How to get there
Rickshaw or CNG to the institute in Rangamati town; it is close to the main town area.
Good to know
Opening hours are limited and it is usually closed on Fridays and public holidays; check locally.

glance: 310 km to Rangamati by road, 8–10 hours by bus or car
dhuppani-waterfall.desc: Dhuppani lies at Orachhari in Farua union of Bilaichhari upazila. The name means 'white water' in the local language, after the white spray of the fall. Getting there means a long boat ride across Kaptai Lake and up the hill rivers, then a walk through forest and hill villages. Because the trip is long, few visitors to Rangamati make it, and the fall is still quiet.
blocks: How to get there
Go from Rangamati or Kaptai by boat to Bilaichhari, register with local authorities, then continue by boat and on foot with a local guide.
Good to know
Bilaichhari is a remote area of the Hill Tracts; check current access rules and carry ID. Go with a local guide and avoid streams in flood.

glance: Naniarchar bazar and the fruit ghats around Rangamati town (Samata Ghat area) in season
naniarchar-pineapple.desc: Naniarchar upazila is Rangamati's pineapple country, and its hills grow several varieties, the best known being the small golden Honey Queen. It is juicy and sweet with little sourness. In season it is sold all over Rangamati town, and a local processing centre has even started making pineapple chips.

glance: Chakma homes during Biju; some indigenous restaurants in Rangamati serve it in April
pajon.desc: Pajon is a slow-cooked mix of seasonal vegetables, roots, young jackfruit, bamboo shoot and herbs, sometimes with dried fish. Traditionally it combines dozens of ingredients and is cooked for the main day of Biju, when households welcome visitors from house to house. It is mild, earthy and believed to be good for health at the start of the new year.

glance: 310 km to Rangamati by road, 8–10 hours by bus or car
furomon-hill.desc: Furomon is one of the higher hills close to Rangamati, rising on the border of Rangamati Sadar and Kaukhali upazilas. A narrow, uneven footpath climbs for two to three hours to the top, where there is an army camp, a Buddha image and a small Buddhist temple. From the summit you see ridges rolling away and, on clear days, parts of Kaptai Lake. It is popular with local trekkers but few outside visitors know about it.
blocks: How to get there
From Rangamati town take a CNG along the Chattogram road toward Sapchhari/Manikchhari and ask for the Furomon trail, then climb on foot.
Good to know
Start early, carry plenty of water and wear good shoes; the path is steep and slippery after rain. Follow instructions at the army camp on top.

biju-boisabi-festival.desc: Boisabi is a combined name for the new-year festivals of the hill communities: Boisu of the Tripura, Sangrai of the Marma and Biju of the Chakma. In Rangamati, Biju begins with Phool Biju, when people float flowers on the lake and rivers at dawn. On the main day, families cook pajon and sweets and visit each other's homes. The festival runs over the last days of Chaitra and the start of Boishakh, in mid-April.
blocks: Good to know
Be a considerate guest; ask before photographing rituals.

glance: Restaurants and cottages in Sajek; order a few hours ahead
sajek-bamboo-chicken.desc: Chicken pieces are marinated with chilli, garlic, ginger and herbs, packed into a length of green bamboo, sealed with leaves and set over the fire. The bamboo steams the meat in its own juices and gives it a faint grassy, smoky flavour. Once a hill-village cooking method, it is now a favourite dinner at Sajek and Rangamati.

glance: 310 km to Rangamati by road, 8–10 hours by bus or car
rangamati-hanging-bridge.desc: The hanging bridge links two hills in the tourism complex at the edge of town, swaying slightly as you walk across. From the middle you look over lake channels and boats. In years of very high water the bridge has been partly submerged, and it has been closed occasionally for repairs. It is busiest in the late afternoon.
blocks: How to get there
In the Parjatan complex on the edge of Rangamati town, a short CNG ride from the bus stand.
Good to know
Go early morning to avoid crowds. Boats for lake trips can be hired nearby.

glance: About 300–450 BDT per kg, depending on size
Samata Ghat area and town bazars in Rangamati, and Naniarchar bazar, in December–January
rangamati-hill-orange.desc: Orange orchards have spread across Naniarchar, Baghaichhari, Bilaichhari, Barkal, Longadu and Juraichhari, with Naniarchar growing the most. The fruit is local komola, a little tart and very fragrant, picked from December to January. Growers bring it by boat to Rangamati town, where you can buy it fresh by the kilo.

glance: 310 km to Rangamati by road, 8–10 hours by bus or car
rajban-vihara.desc: Rajban Vihara is the most important Buddhist temple in the hill tracts, associated with the revered monk Banabhante. The complex includes prayer halls, a tall pagoda and quiet lakeside grounds. Nearby is the residence of the Chakma Circle Chief. It is a peaceful place to understand the faith that shapes daily life for many hill communities.
blocks: How to get there
By CNG within Rangamati town, or by boat across the lake.
Good to know
Dress modestly and remove shoes. Visit during Kathin Chibar Dan for the festival atmosphere.

glance: 310 km to Rangamati by road, 8–10 hours by bus or car
Small entry ticket at the falls (approx.)
shuvolong-waterfall.desc: Shuvolong lies on the way to Barkal, where the lake narrows between steep, forested cliffs. The waterfall pours down a rock face near the water's edge and is at its fullest in the rainy months, dwindling to a trickle by late winter. The boat ride there, between towering hills, is one of the most scenic in the country.
blocks: How to get there
About 1.5 hours by hired boat from Rangamati town.
Good to know
Combine with lunch at an island restaurant and a stop at Rajban Vihara. Skip in dry season if you want to see a big flow.

sajek-valley.desc: Sajek is a string of Lushai and Tripura villages along a high ridge near the Mizoram border, now lined with cottages and cafés. Though it lies in Rangamati district, the road access is from Khagrachhari via Dighinala. The appeal is the view: at dawn, clouds often fill every valley so the surrounding hills seem to float. Helipad and Konglak viewpoints are the classic spots for sunrise and sunset.
blocks: How to get there
From Khagrachhari town, hire a jeep to Baghaihat, then join the army-escorted convoy up to Sajek (about 3 hours in total).
Good to know

Sajek is sometimes closed to tourists at short notice, for heavy rain and landslide risk or during local blockades (it closed in July and again on 11-15 October 2026). Check the Rangamati district administration's latest notice before you go. Vehicles go in escorted convoys at fixed times, so plan around them and carry your ID. Book cottages in advance on weekends. Foreigners need prior permission for the hill tracts, and access has been restricted at times; check current advisories.
